name: Dana Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. I'll describe five pictures of the future and ask what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Brightleaf, a mid-size supermarket in the city centre, mostly evenings from three till eleven. I'm on the tills, but I've ended up as the person who resets the self-checkouts when they freeze, because I'm not scared of the menus. They're also trialling a tall grey robot that rolls down the aisles at night scanning shelves for gaps, and I'm the one who drags it out of the way of the cleaners. I'm still slow on the proper till stuff, like refunds and voids, which embarrasses me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the gadgets, honestly, and the late crowd, nurses after shifts and students buying noodles. What wears me down is being treated like furniture by some customers. Money-wise I'm fine, the evening premium is good and my aunt left me a bit, so I've got well over a year of rent saved. I use AI every day, for translating when a tourist is lost or for my online course in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, if I'm honest, because I like this stuff. At work I'd joke that the grey robot will still need me to rescue it from the mop bucket. Online I'd say the hype people owe everyone an apology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the tills stay much like they are, and I stay the self-checkout fixer. That's fine for now, but I didn't plan to be a cashier at 35. I'd still want to move into something more technical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the online course in electronics I'm doing in the evenings and ask Brightleaf if they have a store systems role. I'd keep my savings invested in the index fund my aunt's money went into. And I'd keep pushing for the staff union to get a seat when they bring in new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a film that ends before the good part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the union matter to you if you're the one who likes the machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm lucky, and lots of my colleagues aren't. Gary on the next till is 50 and can't read the self-checkout screens without his glasses. Someone has to make sure the people like Gary aren't the ones paying for the shiny stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still get on with the till work, the refunds and voids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd have to. I've asked my supervisor Leila to walk me through the refund screen on quiet Mondays. Getting good at the boring bit is part of being taken seriously for the techy bit.

say: I'd admit I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I like the technology.
I'd say the **hype people** owe everyone an apology.
think: The tills stay the same, and I stay the **self-checkout fixer**.
I didn't plan to be a **cashier at 35**, so I'd still move on.
do: Ask Brightleaf about a **store systems** role.
Push for the **staff union** to get a seat on new kit.
feel: **Calm** but a bit flat, like a film ending early.
S0.quote: I didn't plan to be a cashier at 35.
fieldNote: She is **excited by technology** and mildly let down by a plateau.
Her progressive views show in concern for **older colleagues**, not herself.
She works on her **weak till skills** to earn a technical role.

steps.text: Finish the online electronics course this winter
Ask Brightleaf management about a store systems role
Push for a union seat when new kit arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to be smart about it, not scared. I'd post about how shops should train their own staff to run the new kit instead of hiring outside contractors. At work I'd tell people I'll show them the new apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good news. The thinking work that goes first is ordering, rotas and customer emails, and robots come to the shop floor slowly. If I'm the person who keeps the robots running, I'm the last person they cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask head office for a place on their robot maintenance training as soon as it's announced. I'd use AI tools every day to get faster at fault-finding. I'd start a little lunchtime help session for colleagues on the new apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. My worry is for others, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your worry is for others. Who exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary on the next till, and Rosa in customer service, because customer emails and complaints are going to software first. Rosa's good with angry people, but she's not good with computers. I'd want Brightleaf to move Rosa onto something human rather than just cut her hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend any of your savings to get ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd pay for a proper robotics maintenance certificate, it's about two months of rent. With my savings that's an easy bet.

say: I'd say be **smart, not scared** about the change.
I'd argue shops should **train their own staff** instead of hiring contractors.
think: The change is mostly **good news** for me personally.
The person who **keeps robots running** is the last one they cut.
do: Apply for Brightleaf's **robot maintenance** training when it's announced.
Pay for a **robotics certificate** costing about two months' rent.
Run a **lunchtime session** teaching colleagues the new apps.
feel: **Calm**, even a bit **excited**, with worry kept for others.
S1.quote: If I'm the person who keeps the robots running, I'm the last person they cut.
fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as an **opening**, not a threat.
Her concern centres on **Rosa and Gary**, older or less technical staff.

steps.text: Apply for Brightleaf's robot maintenance training
Pay for a robotics maintenance certificate from savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a huge public response, like a guaranteed income or paid retraining for everyone. I'd be posting about it constantly and going to marches. At work I'd stop joking about the grey robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's tighter than I'd like even for me. If robots can do hands-on work as well as people by 2031, they can probably fix each other soon after. My plan to be the robot fixer might only last a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd move straight into a technical role, at Brightleaf or a robot company, and take whatever training they offer. I'd use AI to learn faster than the course allows. I'd keep at least a year of rent in cash and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for this year, but for the year after the year after. I'm good with change, but this is change with no handbrake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a guaranteed income. Would you want that for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it there in case, not as the plan. I'd rather work. But I'd vote for it, because most of the people I work with won't have savings like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Gary, the colleague on the next till?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Gary to talk to the union right away and to use the three years before the robots arrive. And I'd offer to help with his CV. Gary has never written a CV in his life.

say: I'd call for a **huge public response**, like guaranteed income.
I'd go to **marches** and stop joking about the robot.
think: Robots that work as well as people could soon **fix each other**.
My plan to be the **robot fixer** might only last a few years.

Keep **a year of rent** in cash, untouched.
feel: Comfortable with change, but this has **no handbrake**.
S2.quote: I'm good with change, but this is change with no handbrake.
fieldNote: Even this adaptive worker sees her **tech escape route** closing fast.
She backs **guaranteed income** for others while wanting work herself.
Her generosity shows in practical help, like **Gary's CV**.

steps.text: Move into a robot maintenance job within the year
Use AI tutors daily to speed up technical training
Keep a year of rent in cash
March and campaign for paid national retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, if the government starts training people now. I'd be pushing the union to negotiate retraining deals with the big chains. Online I'd share practical stuff, like free courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years plus three before robots means I can get properly qualified and build some experience. Then I'd want to be somewhere that designs or manages the robots, not just resets them. That's a real career if I move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics certificate this year and apply for technician jobs next year. I'd use AI tools every day, and I'd probably invest a bit more of my savings in a part-time engineering diploma. I'd stay at Brightleaf part time while I study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a motivated way. I like a deadline, oddly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the slower version that worries you more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Complacency, at work. With five years, management will say there's plenty of time and then do nothing till year four. I'd want them to start the training now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the city for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, I've got no kids and no mortgage. If a robot company two hours away offered a technician job, I'd go. My flatmate would have to find someone else.

I'd push the union to win **retraining deals** with big chains.
think: I can get **properly qualified** and build experience before 2034.
I'd aim to **design or manage** robots, not just reset them.
do: Finish the **robotics certificate** this year and apply for technician jobs.
Fund a part-time **engineering diploma** from savings.
Stay **part time** at Brightleaf while studying.
feel: **Uneasy** but motivated, because I like a **deadline**.
S3.quote: With five years, management will say there's plenty of time and then do nothing till year four.
fieldNote: She fears **management delay** more than the technology.
With no kids or mortgage she would **move** for work.
She aims higher than repair, toward **managing robots**.

steps.text: Complete the robotics certificate this year
Pay for a part-time engineering diploma
Apply for robot technician jobs, including outside the city
Lobby the union for chain-wide retraining deals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do this right, so let's plan it like grown-ups. I'd talk about it at union meetings and online, mostly about training and fair pay in the new jobs. I'd be more hopeful in public than most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I have time to get a real degree, maybe engineering, and still be early. I'd be 37 when the robots get good. By then I'd want to be on the side that builds and runs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for a part-time engineering degree for next autumn and pay for it with savings. I'd stay at Brightleaf as the store tech while I study. I'd keep using AI every day and try the new kit every chance I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly hopeful. Ten years is a whole career change with time left over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Burnout, maybe, working evenings and studying. I'd drop to four shifts a week, which my savings can cover. I've seen people try to do everything and do nothing well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for colleagues in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper training fund that people can start using now, not in 2035. Gary could retrain at his own pace, and Rosa could too. Ten years is only fair if everyone gets to use it, not just people like me.

say: I'd say we have time to **plan like grown-ups**.
I'd talk about **training and fair pay** in the new jobs.
think: I can get a **real degree** and still be early.
At **37** I'd want to be on the side that builds robots.
do: Apply for a part-time **engineering degree** next autumn.

feel: **Calm** and honestly hopeful about a **career change**.

fieldNote: A long runway makes her **hopeful** and ambitious.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even my plan to fix robots runs out fast. What would help is free technical training for shop workers, starting now, and a basic income floor so nobody's left with nothing. Shops should have to tell staff years ahead when the robots are coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what people are good at that isn't on their job description. My colleague Rosa calms angry customers better than anyone, and no form counts that. Those skills should count when jobs change.

headlineQuote: My colleague Rosa calms angry customers better than anyone, and no form counts that.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old** evening cashier at a city-centre supermarket who resets the **self-checkouts**.
She has over a year of rent saved, helped by an **aunt's inheritance**, and invests it.
She uses AI daily and plans to become a **robot technician** or engineer.
She's calm in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, **anxious** in AGI by 2028, and hopeful with ten years.
Her **progressive** side shows in steady concern for older colleagues like Gary and Rosa.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even her **robot-fixer** plan runs out quickly.
whatWouldHelp: **Free technical training** for shop workers starting now.
A **basic income floor** and early warning from shops about robots.
